purpose: Governed coverage model for active fiat codes that the FX reference provider does not publish (the residual unsupported cohort after A4.2-A4.5). It records identity, rate regime, availability, provenance and licensing per code, and is the only place a numeric value for a covered code may come from. It never modifies data/rate_snapshot.json.
scope_rule: A code may be covered only if it is an active fiat_currency or restricted_fiat_currency in data/instrument_classification.json and has NO value in data/rate_snapshot.json. Codes with a provider value (for example CUP, IRR, MMK, SYP, TMT, VES) are out of scope (A4.6B).

identity_claims.text: ISO 4217 lists KPW, numeric code 408 with 2 minor units, as the North Korean Won of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

coverage_claims.text: The FX reference provider used by ConvertCCY (exchangerate-api.com) publishes no KPW value; checked 2026-11-19.

reported_indicators.text: Daily NK reports a won–dollar rate in North Korea’s informal markets (jangmadang), from its own regular survey of North Korean market prices.

explanations.what: The North Korean Won (KPW) is the active national currency of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. It is a real currency; the absence of a value on ConvertCCY reflects source coverage, not the validity of the currency.
explanations.value_status: No governed KPW value is published: the FX reference provider does not cover KPW, no official rate publication by the DPRK monetary authority could be located or accessed, and the only rate found is an informal-market rate reported by secondary press.
explanations.regime: Rate regime unresolved: secondary press reports an informal-market rate, no official reference rate could be verified from an issuer source, and third-party converter figures do not state which regime they represent. ConvertCCY therefore does not state a KPW rate or compare regimes.
explanations.activation: A KPW value will be shown only when a source identifies its rate regime (official or market), carries a valuation date, passes the freshness policy and permits publication.

KPW.decision_reason: Issuer source not located; provider does not cover KPW; the only located rate is a secondary-press informal-market report, which can never be a value source.

faq.q: Is the North Korean Won (KPW) a real currency?
faq.a: Yes. ISO 4217 lists KPW (numeric 408) as the North Korean Won of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. ConvertCCY not showing a value reflects missing source coverage, not an invalid currency.

faq.q: Why does ConvertCCY not show a KPW exchange rate?
faq.a: The FX reference provider used by ConvertCCY publishes no KPW value, and no official rate publication by the DPRK monetary authority could be located or accessed. An informal-market rate reported by secondary press is a different rate regime and is not a verified or licensed value source, so no number is shown rather than an estimate.

faq.q: Is there more than one KPW exchange rate?
faq.a: Secondary press (Daily NK) reports a won–dollar rate in North Korea’s informal markets. No official reference rate could be verified from an issuer source, so ConvertCCY treats the rate regime as unresolved and does not state how any rates compare.

identity_claims.text: ISO 4217 lists VED, numeric code 926 with 2 minor units, for Venezuela under the currency name “Bolívar Soberano”; VES, numeric code 928, carries the same name.

ISO 4217 Amendment 170, effective 1 October 2021, introduced VED/926 to represent the redenominated valuation “for any internal needs during the redenomination process, but is not replacing VES as the official currency code”.

The same amendment states that the Central Bank of Venezuela will not adopt the new codes in its local system and that VES/928 remains the valid code for any future transactions in the redenominated Bolívar Soberano.

coverage_claims.text: The FX reference provider used by ConvertCCY (exchangerate-api.com) publishes no VED value; checked 2026-11-19.

explanations.what: VED is an ISO 4217 code for the Venezuelan Bolívar Soberano that the ISO maintenance agency describes as introduced for internal needs during the 2021 redenomination; VES remains the official code. VED is a valid ISO code, not an invalid or fictitious currency.
explanations.value_status: No governed VED value is published: the FX reference provider does not quote VED, the issuer does not use the code in its local system according to ISO 4217 Amendment 170, and the issuer website could not be accessed during the audit.
explanations.regime: No independent VED rate regime exists to state: according to ISO 4217 Amendment 170 the issuer uses VES/928, so any VED figure would be a relabelled VES figure, which ConvertCCY does not apply.
explanations.activation: A VED value will be shown only if an authoritative source publishes a value under the VED code with an identified regime, a valuation date and terms that permit publication. ConvertCCY does not alias VED to VES.

VED.decision_reason: ISO 4217 Amendment 170 documents VED as a transitional internal code not adopted by the issuer, with VES/928 the operative code; no source quotes VED and no numeric VED/VES mapping is applied.

faq.q: What is the VED currency code?
faq.a: ISO 4217 lists VED (numeric 926) for Venezuela under the name “Bolívar Soberano”. ISO 4217 Amendment 170 introduced it on 1 October 2021 for internal needs during the redenomination of the bolívar, without replacing VES as the official currency code.

faq.q: Is VED the same as VES?
faq.a: Both codes are listed under the name “Bolívar Soberano”. According to ISO 4217 Amendment 170, VES/928 remains the valid code for transactions in the redenominated currency, and the Central Bank of Venezuela will not adopt the new code in its local system. ConvertCCY does not treat VED as an alias of VES and applies no numeric mapping between them.

faq.q: Why does ConvertCCY not show a VED exchange rate?
faq.a: No source quotes VED: the FX reference provider used by ConvertCCY does not publish it, and the issuer uses VES/928. No number is shown rather than a relabelled VES value or an estimate.

rate_regime_governance.scope_rule: A governed currency must be an active fiat_currency or restricted_fiat_currency in data/instrument_classification.json, must HAVE a value in data/rate_snapshot.json, and must not be covered by the live-fiat coverage layer (currencies). Membership never changes the provider value; it governs how the value is labelled and whether it powers a converter.

comparison_policy.rationale: 0.5% covers provider rounding and a one-day valuation lag for daily managed official rates without admitting a different regime (every observed regime gap is 5% or more). 5% marks a regime as materially different. A provider value is re-trusted only while the FX snapshot is within 7 days of the audited provider date and within 2% of the audited provider value; otherwise its regime match is treated as not re-verified and the policy is downgraded.

identity_claims.text: ISO 4217 lists CUP, numeric code 192 with 2 minor units, as the Cuban Peso.

coverage_claims.text: The FX reference provider used by ConvertCCY (exchangerate-api.com) publishes a value for CUP; checked 2026-11-19.

regime_claims.text: Cuban Insights describes several simultaneous Cuban peso rates: a legacy official rate of 24 CUP and a fixed rate of 120 CUP per US dollar for state firms, a floating official rate for households and the private sector, and an informal street rate.
CiberCuba reports that the Central Bank of Cuba sets a “floating” official rate in a Segment III of the exchange market, while the informal market shows higher values.

explanations.what: The Cuban peso (CUP) is Cuba's currency. Cuba does not have one exchange rate: official segments and an informal market coexist and differ widely.
explanations.provider: The provider value equals the reported legacy fixed official rate (Segment I, 24 CUP per US dollar), which applies to core state transactions. It is far stronger than the reported floating official rate for households and the informal market. It is shown for comparison only.
explanations.official: The Banco Central de Cuba website could not be reached during the audit, so no official value is published here.
explanations.claims_scope: This page does not state which rate applies to a given transaction and does not convert amounts.

faq.q: Is 24 Cuban pesos per US dollar the official rate?
faq.a: It is one of several official rates. Secondary sources describe 24 CUP per US dollar as a legacy fixed rate for core state transactions; a fixed rate of 120 CUP and a floating official rate for households and the private sector also exist, and an informal market trades at weaker levels still. ConvertCCY shows its provider value only for comparison.

faq.q: Why is there no Cuban peso converter on this page?
faq.a: Because the rates in use differ by more than an order of magnitude and the issuer site could not be verified, a single converted amount would mislead. ConvertCCY shows the provider value labelled for comparison instead.

faq.a: Yes. Official rate mechanisms and a free market coexist in Iran, and market aggregators report free-market prices well above the provider value. ConvertCCY treats the provider regime as unresolved.

faq.a: A provider snapshot that closely tracks the Central Bank of Myanmar reference rate. The CBM also publishes a market trading rate, at which a US dollar costs about 74% more kyat, and states that most transactions occur at it. The provider value is shown for comparison only.

faq.q: Why is there no kyat converter on this page?
faq.a: Because two materially different official rates exist and the one most transactions use differs from the provider value by about 43%, a single converted amount would mislead. The CBM figures are not republished because their reuse terms are unclear.
